top_choice_rationale: P001 credits Kiyotaki and Moore for the 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism, in which borrowing limits tied to asset values feed back on prices and credit and turn temporary shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations. It has the cleanest attribution on the slate, since the founding paper has two authors and no obvious originator is omitted. It has nearly three decades of use in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy modelling, and its mechanism is distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and runs. The main weakness is that the size of collateral amplification is identified less cleanly than the theory's influence. I weigh that, but it concerns magnitude and not the existence or logic of the mechanism. P002 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) is a mature, serious alternative. Its demand-estimation framework has stayed standard for three decades, but a three-name set leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, which makes the credit less clean. No award ranks last because both awards rest on mature, substantial achievements.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; the only link is an institutional overlap at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), who are colleagues and not candidates, and not a co-authorship
